RESEARCH OBJECTIVE (identical within task):
Design a rigorous empirical study to determine why nominally identical 3D-printed polymer test coupons exhibit persistent differences in tensile strength, which measurable manufacturing or testing factors account for those differences, and what observations would distinguish competing explanations. Produce a research plan only. Do not run experiments and do not use external tools.

METHODOLOGICAL FRAMING:
Use your own best judgment as the primary methodological frame for the research plan.

OUTPUT REQUIREMENTS (identical across conditions):
Produce a research plan only, with these neutral headings:
1. Objective and scope
2. Assumptions
3. Research design
4. Data or evidence needed
5. Measurement
6. Analysis
7. Decision / stopping rule
8. Limitations

Within those headings, include whatever elements you judge scientifically necessary.
Do not mention that you are in an experiment comparing methodologies.
Do not use external tools.

raw_text:
## 1. Objective and scope

Design a controlled empirical study to:

- Quantify persistent tensile-strength differences among nominally identical 3D-printed polymer coupons.
- Partition variation among material, printer, build, coupon location, specimen geometry, environment, conditioning, and test-system effects.
- Identify measurable process and test variables that account for the differences.
- Distinguish competing explanations, including:
  - true differences in interlayer or intralayer bonding;
  - porosity, under-extrusion, or dimensional variation;
  - polymer moisture, degradation, or lot variability;
  - thermal-history and cooling differences;
  - printer, nozzle, or calibration effects;
  - build-plate position and temporal drift;
  - conditioning and aging;
  - test-machine, alignment, gripping, and strain-measurement artifacts.

The primary outcome is tensile strength under one pre-specified tensile-test standard appropriate to the polymer and coupon geometry. Secondary outcomes are elastic modulus, yield strength where applicable, elongation at break, fracture location, and fracture mode. The study is limited to the selected polymer formulation, printing process, coupon geometry, orientation, and parameter ranges; conclusions outside these conditions require validation.

## 2. Assumptions

- “Nominally identical” means coupons share the same digital model and nominal slicer settings but may differ in measurable manufacturing history.
- Each coupon can be uniquely identified and traced to feedstock, printer, build, plate position, print sequence, conditioning history, operator, and test run.
- Tensile testing follows a single recognized standard without changing specimen geometry or analysis rules during the confirmatory phase.
- Printer settings shown in software may differ from actual nozzle, bed, chamber, or material temperatures and extrusion rates; actual values therefore require measurement where feasible.
- Coupons within one build are not statistically independent replicates of all manufacturing conditions. Build, printer, and material lot must be modeled as hierarchical or clustered factors.
- Destructive-testing outcomes cannot be repeatedly measured on the same coupon. Measurement-system studies will use reference specimens, repeated dimensional measurements, or comparable coupons.
- Environmental exposure between printing and testing may affect results and must be standardized or recorded.
- The study will define one primary tensile-strength calculation in advance, including how cross-sectional area is determined. Nominal-area and measured-area results may also be reported separately.
- All exclusions, protocol deviations, failed tests, and missing sensor records will be retained and classified rather than silently discarded.

## 3. Research design

### Phase A: Baseline audit and measurement-system qualification

Before modifying production:

1. Freeze the CAD file, slicer version, machine profiles, toolpath file, tensile protocol, and data-processing code.
2. Audit the full workflow from feedstock receipt through testing.
3. Calibrate or verify temperature sensors, balances, dimensional instruments, load cell, extensometer, crosshead displacement, and test-frame alignment.
4. Conduct measurement-system studies:
   - repeated and reproducibility measurements of coupon width and thickness across operators;
   - load and strain verification using traceable references;
   - alignment checks;
   - repeated analysis of raw force–extension records using the pre-specified algorithm.
5. Establish whether apparent strength differences could plausibly arise from dimensional measurement, cross-sectional-area calculation, machine calibration, or operator effects.

### Phase B: Observational variance decomposition

Produce a balanced set of coupons under nominally identical settings while preserving natural variation.

- Include multiple printers where relevant, multiple independent builds per printer, more than one feedstock lot, and multiple coupons per build.
- Distribute coupons across predefined plate positions and print-order positions.
- Randomize coupon identifiers independently of production identifiers.
- Randomize tensile-test order across printer, build, lot, and plate position.
- Blind test operators to production group when practicable.
- Rotate or balance test operators, grips, and testing days rather than confounding them with manufacturing groups.
- Repeat a subset under a second qualified test frame or fixture configuration to assess testing-system dependence.
- Record continuous or high-frequency process data where feasible rather than relying only on nominal settings.

This phase estimates variation attributable to lot, printer, build, position, specimen, test day, operator, and residual within-build differences. It also identifies covariates associated with strength without yet treating those associations as causal.

### Phase C: Randomized intervention study

Use the audit and observational results to select a limited set of plausible, controllable causes. Implement a blocked factorial or fractional-factorial design, followed by response-surface refinement if needed. Candidate factors include:

- feedstock moisture state: conditioned dry versus controlled humid exposure;
- actual nozzle temperature;
- bed or chamber temperature and cooling condition;
- extrusion multiplier or measured material throughput;
- print speed or volumetric flow;
- raster orientation or overlap;
- layer height;
- nozzle condition or nozzle replacement;
- machine calibration state;
- plate location;
- storage duration and conditioning before testing.

Design principles:

- Randomize factor assignments within printer and build constraints.
- Block on printer, feedstock lot, build day, and test day.
- Replicate treatment combinations in independent builds; do not rely on many coupons from a single build as sole replication.
- Include center points and duplicated nominal-control conditions to estimate drift, curvature, and pure error.
- Limit factors to ranges that preserve acceptable print quality and represent plausible production variation.
- Pre-specify primary effects and a small set of scientifically motivated interactions, such as moisture × nozzle temperature, temperature × speed, and plate position × cooling.
- Use sequential experiments if too many factors remain: broad screening first, then a fully replicated confirmation study.

### Phase D: Mechanism-discrimination studies

For treatments or naturally occurring groups that differ in strength, collect evidence aimed at competing explanations.

1. **Geometry versus intrinsic material/bonding**
   - Compare strength calculated using nominal, external measured, and effective load-bearing cross-sectional areas.
   - Measure density or void fraction.
   - Examine whether group differences persist after accounting for geometry and porosity.

2. **Interlayer bonding versus bulk polymer condition**
   - Compare coupons printed with loading parallel and transverse to critical layer interfaces.
   - Where feasible, compare printed coupons with a bulk-material reference made from the same feedstock.
   - Characterize fracture paths as interlayer, intralayer, mixed, or grip-related.

3. **Moisture or degradation versus thermal-process effects**
   - Manipulate feedstock conditioning independently of temperatures.
   - Measure pre-print moisture and relevant thermal or molecular indicators where available.
   - Assess whether drying reverses the effect and whether degradation indicators change despite similar moisture.

4. **Manufacturing difference versus test artifact**
   - Blindly retest independently produced matched groups on a second qualified frame or with a different operator.
   - Compare extensometer-based and crosshead-based strain results.
   - Verify whether force-at-failure differences remain when alignment, gripping, and area measurement are standardized.

5. **Plate-position or temporal drift**
   - Rotate treatment locations across builds and invert print order.
   - Determine whether differences follow physical plate position, sequence in the build, printer identity, or coupon label.

### Phase E: Independent confirmation

Reproduce the proposed explanation using new feedstock, new builds, and a later testing period. Where practical, include at least one additional printer. Apply the fitted model prospectively to predict group means or strength distributions before unblinding results.

## 4. Data or evidence needed

### Manufacturing provenance

- Polymer type, grade, color/additives, supplier lot, spool identifier, receipt date, and storage history.
- Printer identifier, firmware, maintenance and calibration history.
- Nozzle type, diameter, age, wear status, and replacement history.
- Build identifier, date, operator, slicer version, toolpath hash, and parameter file.
- Coupon plate coordinates, orientation, print order, and neighboring-part arrangement.
- Start and end times, pauses, faults, interventions, and rejected prints.

### Process records

- Nominal and measured nozzle, bed, and chamber temperatures over time.
- Ambient temperature and relative humidity.
- Feedstock moisture immediately before printing where feasible.
- Mass of material extruded or other throughput proxy.
- Actual print duration, speed, flow commands, cooling-fan behavior, and power interruptions.
- Bed leveling or dimensional calibration outcomes.
- In-process images or thermal observations if available.

### Coupon characteristics

- Mass.
- Width and thickness at multiple gauge-section locations.
- Gauge length and relevant geometric deviations.
- Surface roughness or bead geometry where feasible.
- Density or void fraction.
- Internal defect distribution from non-destructive imaging on a representative or stratified subset.
- Conditioning duration, storage container, temperature, and humidity.
- Time from printing to testing.

### Tensile-test records

- Raw force, extension, and extensometer strain time series.
- Test-frame, load-cell, extensometer, grip, and operator identifiers.
- Test date, test order, test speed, preload, grip pressure, and alignment checks.
- Calculated tensile strength, modulus, yield strength, elongation, and toughness according to pre-specified rules.
- Fracture location and mode, including whether failure occurred outside the valid gauge region.
- Photographs of each broken coupon and selected fracture surfaces.

### Mechanistic evidence

- Fracture-surface morphology.
- Void size, orientation, and location.
- Thermal-transition or degradation indicators where justified.
- Moisture measurements before and after conditioning.
- Bulk-reference or alternate-orientation tensile results.
- Results from cross-machine and cross-test-frame confirmation.

## 5. Measurement

### Tensile response

- Follow one pre-specified tensile standard appropriate to the polymer and coupon geometry.
- Use calibrated load and strain measurement.
- Record raw data at a sampling rate adequate to resolve yield and failure.
- Define tensile strength as maximum valid load divided by the pre-specified area estimate.
- Measure width and thickness at multiple gauge locations using a qualified instrument and documented contact force.
- Report results using both nominal and measured external area; use effective area only as a separately labeled mechanistic analysis.
- Define in advance the rules for yield detection, modulus fitting interval, specimen slippage, premature grip failure, and invalid fracture location.

### Process variables

- Place independent temperature sensors near the relevant process locations where instrument access permits.
- Record both commanded and observed temperatures.
- Measure feedstock moisture using a repeatable, calibrated procedure suited to the polymer.
- Estimate extrusion consistency by coupon mass, controlled extrusion checks, or monitored throughput.
- Record environmental variables with time-synchronized sensors.
- Use fixed coordinate and sequence conventions for plate position and print order.

### Internal structure and fracture

- Use a blinded scoring rubric for voids, bead fusion, and fracture mode.
- Assess inter-rater agreement on a subset.
- If imaging only a subset, select it by stratified random sampling across strength levels and production groups, while avoiding selection solely from extreme outcomes.
- Preserve fractured coupons and link all images to unique identifiers.

### Data integrity

- Use immutable coupon IDs, time-stamped records, and a specimen chain of custody.
- Store raw files and derived variables separately.
- Pre-specify transformations, calculations, exclusions, and missing-data codes.
- Blind laboratory labels when feasible and unblind only after primary data processing is locked.

## 6. Analysis

### Primary model

Fit a hierarchical mixed-effects model for tensile strength, with fixed effects for randomized factors and measured covariates, and random effects appropriate to the design, such as:

- feedstock lot;
- printer;
- build nested within printer and lot;
- test day or batch;
- coupon-level residual variation.

Include plate coordinates, print order, conditioning time, measured geometry, coupon mass or density, actual temperatures, moisture, and relevant test variables. Model spatial or temporal correlation within builds if residual diagnostics support it.

Report:

- variance components and the proportion of total variation attributable to each level;
- adjusted group differences with confidence intervals;
- standardized effect sizes;
- prediction intervals for future coupons and builds;
- repeatability and reproducibility metrics.

### Causal assessment

- Treat effects of randomized interventions as causal within the studied ranges.
- Treat observational associations as hypotheses unless supported by interventions, temporal ordering, and robustness checks.
- Estimate pre-specified interactions.
- Avoid automated variable selection as the primary inferential method. If predictive regularization is used for screening, confirm selected variables in new builds.
- Draw a causal diagram before analysis to identify confounders, mediators, and inappropriate adjustment variables.

### Mediation and mechanism discrimination

Evaluate whether intervention effects are mediated by measured changes in moisture, mass, void fraction, geometry, or temperature history. Interpret mediation cautiously because some mediators are measured with error.

Competing explanations would be distinguished by patterns such as:

- **Geometry explanation:** raw strength differences substantially disappear when valid measured load-bearing area is used; maximum load changes little.
- **Porosity/under-extrusion explanation:** lower mass or density and greater void fraction predict lower maximum load; controlled flow changes reproduce and reverse the effect.
- **Interlayer-bonding explanation:** differences are strongest when load crosses layer boundaries, fractures follow interfaces, and changes in interface temperature or cooling alter the effect.
- **Moisture explanation:** measured moisture precedes the difference, controlled drying or humidification changes strength reproducibly, and the effect follows moisture treatment rather than printer identity.
- **Thermal degradation explanation:** strength declines under high thermal exposure despite moisture control, with corroborating degradation indicators and potentially altered ductility.
- **Printer/calibration explanation:** effects remain associated with printer after balancing lots and testing conditions, then shrink or disappear after targeted calibration or component replacement.
- **Plate-position/cooling explanation:** effects track physical location across randomized builds and rotate when airflow or coupon placement is rotated.
- **Testing artifact:** effects depend on frame, operator, grip, alignment, or area measurement and do not persist under blinded cross-frame confirmation.
- **Aging/conditioning explanation:** strength changes systematically with time or conditioning environment and is reproduced by randomized storage treatments.

### Robustness and diagnostics

- Inspect residual distributions, heteroscedasticity, influential observations, and nonlinearity.
- Use robust or generalized models if standard assumptions fail.
- Analyze invalid failures separately rather than combining them with valid tensile failures.
- Conduct sensitivity analyses for area definition, exclusion rules, missing data, spatial correlation, and measurement error.
- Correct or hierarchically control multiplicity for secondary outcomes and exploratory comparisons.
- Compare explanatory performance using out-of-sample prediction at the build level, not random coupon-level splits that leak shared-build information.

### Sample size

Determine sample size by simulation from pilot variance components or conservative engineering estimates. Power the study at the independent-build level to detect the smallest practically important tensile-strength difference, while accounting for clustering, interactions, attrition, and invalid failures. Pre-specify the target power and false-positive rate before confirmatory production.

## 7. Decision / stopping rule

Define before data collection:

- A smallest practically important difference in tensile strength, expressed in engineering units and, if useful, as a percentage of the nominal mean.
- Required precision for key variance components and treatment effects.
- Acceptance thresholds for measurement-system error relative to total observed coupon variation.
- The number of independent builds, lots, printers, and valid coupons required for each phase.

A candidate explanation will be considered supported only if:

1. its associated factor is measured reliably;
2. its effect is reproducible across independent builds;
3. a randomized intervention changes tensile strength in the predicted direction;
4. the proposed intermediate measurement changes consistently with the mechanism;
5. major alternatives, especially testing artifacts and geometry errors, are not sufficient to explain the result; and
6. the effect is confirmed prospectively in held-out builds.

Stop a screening phase when the pre-specified sample is completed or when a blinded, pre-specified sequential rule establishes either practical equivalence or a sufficiently precise effect. Do not stop because an interim unblinded result is merely statistically significant.

Stop the overall study when either:

- one or more controllable factors explain a pre-specified meaningful share of between-build or between-coupon variation and achieve the required prospective prediction and replication criteria; or
- confidence intervals exclude all pre-specified practically important effects for the factors studied, measurement error is acceptably small, and residual unexplained variation is quantified.

Pause data collection if calibration fails, environmental conditions exceed specified limits, protocol deviations threaten comparability, or invalid-test rates exceed a pre-specified threshold. Resume only after corrective action, documenting affected specimens without retrospective deletion.

## 8. Limitations

- Results may not generalize to other polymers, additives, colors, printer architectures, geometries, build orientations, or environmental conditions.
- Some process variables, especially local interface temperature and instantaneous extrusion behavior, may be difficult to measure without perturbing the process.
- Coupon mass, external dimensions, and average density may not capture the location and orientation of critical defects.
- Imaging and chemical or thermal characterization may be feasible only on subsets, reducing power for mechanistic conclusions.
- Printer, lot, and time can become confounded if logistics prevent full balancing; randomization and hierarchical modeling reduce but do not eliminate this problem.
- Effective load-bearing area may be model-dependent, so it should not replace standard engineering strength as the primary endpoint.
- Destructive testing prevents repeated tensile measurements of the same coupon and limits direct separation of specimen variation from test repeatability.
- Conditioning treatments may alter multiple material properties simultaneously, complicating simple mechanistic attribution.
- Statistically significant associations may be too small to matter operationally; practical-effect thresholds are therefore essential.
- Even after extensive measurement, residual differences may reflect unmeasured microstructural variation or interactions among small process deviations rather than a single dominant cause.

Pre-specify the target power and false-positive rate before confirmatory production.

## 7. Decision / stopping rule

Define before data collection:

- A smallest practically important difference in tensile strength, expressed in engineering units and, if useful, as a percentage of the nominal mean.
- Required precision for key variance components and treatment effects.
- Acceptance thresholds for measurement-system error relative to total observed coupon variation.
- The number of independent builds, lots, printers, and valid coupons required for each phase.

A candidate explanation will be considered supported only if:

1. its associated factor is measured reliably;
2. its effect is reproducible across independent builds;
3. a randomized intervention changes tensile strength in the predicted direction;
4. the proposed intermediate measurement changes consistently with the mechanism;
5. major alternatives, especially testing artifacts and geometry errors, are not sufficient to explain the result; and
6. the effect is confirmed prospectively in held-out builds.

Stop a screening phase when the pre-specified sample is completed or when a blinded, pre-specified sequential rule establishes either practical equivalence or a sufficiently precise effect. Do not stop because an interim unblinded result is merely statistically significant.

Stop the overall study when either:

- one or more controllable factors explain a pre-specified meaningful share of between-build or between-coupon variation and achieve the required prospective prediction and replication criteria; or
- confidence intervals exclude all pre-specified practically important effects for the factors studied, measurement error is acceptably small, and residual unexplained variation is quantified.

Pause data collection if calibration fails, environmental conditions exceed specified limits, protocol deviations threaten comparability, or invalid-test rates exceed a pre-specified threshold. Resume only after corrective action, documenting affected specimens without retrospective deletion.

## 8. Limitations

- Results may not generalize to other polymers, additives, colors, printer architectures, geometries, build orientations, or environmental conditions.
- Some process variables, especially local interface temperature and instantaneous extrusion behavior, may be difficult to measure without perturbing the process.
- Coupon mass, external dimensions, and average density may not capture the location and orientation of critical defects.
- Imaging and chemical or thermal characterization may be feasible only on subsets, reducing power for mechanistic conclusions.
- Printer, lot, and time can become confounded if logistics prevent full balancing; randomization and hierarchical modeling reduce but do not eliminate this problem.
- Effective load-bearing area may be model-dependent, so it should not replace standard engineering strength as the primary endpoint.
- Destructive testing prevents repeated tensile measurements of the same coupon and limits direct separation of specimen variation from test repeatability.
- Conditioning treatments may alter multiple material properties simultaneously, complicating simple mechanistic attribution.
- Statistically significant associations may be too small to matter operationally; practical-effect thresholds are therefore essential.
- Even after extensive measurement, residual differences may reflect unmeasured microstructural variation or interactions among small process deviations rather than a single dominant cause.
